claim: Bacterial pathogens are leading causes of global infectious disease burden, with antibiotic-resistant and healthcare-associated infections posing significant risks to patient safety and public health.
source: Bacteria are fundamental drivers of human health and disease. On one hand, bacterial pathogens are leading causes of global infectious disease burden, with antibiotic-resistant and healthcare-associated infections posing significant risks to patient safety and public health (Cassini et al., 2019; Cassini et al., 2016; Friedman et al., 2016; Naylor et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature on infectious disease burden and antibiotic resistance.

claim: The bacterial microbiome provides support to development and homeostasis, facilitates core physiological processes like digestion, and protects against diseases ranging from colitis to cancer.
source: On the other, the bacterial microbiome – the trillions of individual bacteria that collectively inhabit the human body – provides support to development and homeostasis, facilitates core physiological processes like digestion, and protects against diseases ranging from colitis to cancer (Bäckhed et al., 2005; Kamada et al., 2013b; Lynch and Pedersen, 2016; Round and Mazmanian, 2009; Roy and Trinchieri, 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research on microbiome functions.

claim: The microbiome can protect against colonization with infectious bacterial pathogens through colonization resistance, limiting their capacities to establish colonies, grow, persist, and transmit.
source: The microbiome can also protect against colonization with infectious bacterial pathogens, a phenomenon known as colonization resistance, limiting their capacities to establish colonies, grow, persist, and transmit (Bäumler and Sperandio, 2016; Buffie and Pamer, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research on colonization resistance.

claim: Growth of Clostridioides difficile within the intestine is inhibited by secondary metabolites of commensal gut bacteria, protecting colonized hosts from disease and limiting propagation of infectious spores.
source: This is perhaps best exemplified by the canonical Clostridioides difficile: growth within the intestine is inhibited by secondary metabolites of commensal gut bacteria, protecting colonized hosts from disease and limiting propagation of the infectious spores that drive between-host transmission (Kamada et al., 2013a; Pamer, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research on C. difficile and microbiome interactions.

claim: Antibiotics can unintentionally destabilize healthy microbial communities when prescribed, resulting in dysbiosis.
source: When prescribed appropriately, antibiotics target particular bacterial pathogens, but co-colonizing microbiota are also exposed (Tedijanto et al., 2018). This can unintentionally destabilize healthy microbial communities, resulting in dysbiosis, a state of population dynamic disequilibrium (Bhalodi et al., 2019; Coyte et al., 2015; Dethlefsen and Relman, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research on antibiotic effects on microbiota.

claim: Microbiome dysbiosis is associated with reduced abundance and diversity of commensal bacteria, impaired host immune responses, and loss of colonization resistance, increasing host susceptibility to ARB colonization.
source: Microbiome dysbiosis is associated with reduced abundance and diversity of commensal bacteria, impaired host immune responses, and loss of colonization resistance, altogether increasing host susceptibility to ARB colonization (Kim et al., 2017; Sorbara and Pamer, 2019; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research on dysbiosis and ARB susceptibility.

claim: Antibiotic-induced dysbiosis may result in elevated expression of antibiotic resistance genes, increased rates of horizontal transfer of such genes, and ecological release of subdominant ARB.
source: Antibiotic-induced dysbiosis may further result in elevated expression of antibiotic resistance genes, increased rates of horizontal transfer of such genes, and ecological release, whereby subdominant ARB are released from competition via clearance of drug-sensitive bacteria, growing out into dominant colonies (Doan et al., 2019; Letten et al., 2021; Ruppé et al., 2019; Stecher et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research on dysbiosis effects on resistance.

claim: Microbiome dysbiosis is increasingly recognized as a key driver of ARB colonization and infection in healthcare settings where antibiotic use is widespread.
source: These associations may be particularly relevant for healthcare settings, where antibiotic use is widespread, and where microbiome dysbiosis is increasingly recognized as a key driver of ARB colonization and infection (Baggs et al., 2018; Prescott et al., 2015; Ravi et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research on healthcare-associated infections and dysbiosis.

claim: Most epidemiological models consider just one species of bacteria at a time, under the assumption that antibiotic selection for resistance results from intraspecific competition between co-circulating strains.
source: Disruption of the host microbiome is a long-standing theory explaining how antibiotics select for the spread of resistance at both the individual and population levels (Lipsitch and Samore, 2002), but most epidemiological models consider just one species of bacteria at a time, under the traditional assumption that antibiotic selection for resistance results from intraspecific competition between co-circulating strains (Blanquart, 2019; Ramsay et al., 2018; Spicknall et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published modeling literature and theoretical frameworks.

claim: The simple strain competition framework has been particularly useful for bacteria like Streptococcus pneumoniae and Staphylococcus aureus, where different strains are believed to be in close ecological competition.
source: This simple framework has been particularly useful for bacteria like Streptococcus pneumoniae and Staphylococcus aureus, in which different strains – sometimes conceptualized as drug-sensitive vs. drug-resistant, or community-associated vs. healthcare-associated – are believed to be in close ecological competition (Blanquart, 2019; Domenech de Cellès et al., 2011; Kardaś-Słoma et al., 2011; Pressley et al., 2010; van Kleef et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published modeling studies on specific bacterial species.

claim: Within-host bacterial competition remains a key mechanism of selection for antibiotic resistance dissemination and an active area of research in resistance modeling.
source: Nevertheless, within-host bacterial competition remains a key mechanism of selection for antibiotic resistance dissemination, and an active area of research at the forefront of resistance modeling (Lipsitch and Samore, 2002; Mulberry et al., 2020; Spicknall et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research on within-host competition and resistance modeling.

claim: The 'mixed-carriage' model by Davies et al. demonstrates how intraspecific competition results in negative frequency-dependent selection for either of two competing strains and provides a mechanistic explanation for widespread strain coexistence at the population level.
source: For instance, the 'mixed-carriage' model by Davies et al. demonstrates how intraspecific competition results in negative frequency-dependent selection for either of two competing strains, and provides a satisfying mechanistic explanation for widespread strain coexistence at the population level (Davies et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to a specific published model by Davies et al.

claim: Contemporary work has stopped short of evaluating consequences of between-species competition on resistance epidemiology.
source: However, contemporary work has stopped short of evaluating consequences of between-species competition on resistance epidemiology.
evidence: Based on the authors' assessment of the current state of the literature.

claim: For many ARB, including ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae, interactions with the host microbiome may be important mediators of nosocomial colonization dynamics.
source: Yet for many ARB, including emerging high-priority multidrug-resistant bacteria like extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) producing Enterobacteriaceae, interactions with the host microbiome may be important mediators of nosocomial colonization dynamics (Kim et al., 2017; Lerminiaux and Cameron, 2019; Pilmis et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research on Enterobacteriaceae and microbiome interactions.

claim: When PR is resistant to all antibiotics (rR = 1), its prevalence increases monotonically with increasing antibiotic exposure.
source: Unlike the single-strain Susceptible-Colonized model (Figure 1D and G), the strain competition model can explain how antibiotic consumption selects for the spread of resistance (Figures 1E,H). When PR is resistant to all antibiotics (rR = 1), its prevalence increases monotonically with increasing antibiotic exposure (Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: Supported by model results shown in referenced figures.

claim: When resistance is partial (0 < rR < 1), selection for resistance can peak at intermediate antibiotic exposure, owing to a trade-off in how antibiotics both clear and facilitate PR.
source: When resistance is partial – when PR is still cleared by antibiotics, but at a lower rate than PS (rS < rR < 1) – selection for resistance can peak at intermediate antibiotic exposure, owing to a trade-off in how antibiotics both clear and facilitate PR.
evidence: Supported by model results and mechanistic reasoning.

claim: R0 for PR tends to increase with antibiotic use when PR is highly resistant to antibiotics (high rR), but decrease when still largely sensitive (low rR).
source: As such, R0 for PR tends to increase with antibiotic use when PR is highly resistant to antibiotics (high rR), but decrease when still largely sensitive (low rR).
evidence: Supported by model results and mechanistic reasoning.

claim: A stable microbiome can act as a barrier preventing introduced pathogens from establishing colonies through colonization resistance (ε).
source: First, a stable microbiome can act as a barrier preventing introduced pathogens from establishing colonies. We modeled this colonization resistance (ε) as a reduced rate of pathogen transmission (β) to hosts with stable microbiota, βε = (1 – ε) × β.
evidence: Supported by citations to published research and formalized in the model.

claim: Co-colonizing bacteria can compete for space, nutrients and other limited resources within the host through resource competition (η).
source: Second, co-colonizing bacteria can compete for space, nutrients and other limited resources within the host. In this case, antibiotics that reduce the density of potential competitors may favour pathogen persistence. We modeled this resource competition (η) as a reduced rate of pathogen clearance (γ) among hosts undergoing dysbiosis, γη = (1 – η) × γ.
evidence: Supported by citations to published research and formalized in the model.

claim: Microbiome dysbiosis can favor the emergence or outgrowth of subdominant pathogen colonies through ecological release (ϕ).
source: Lastly, microbiome dysbiosis can favor the emergence or outgrowth of subdominant pathogen colonies, and this ecological release (ϕ) was modeled as an increased rate of endogenous pathogen acquisition (α) upon dysbiosis, αϕ = ϕ × α.
evidence: Supported by citations to published research and formalized in the model.

claim: Microbiome competition underlies a trade-off in antibiotic selection where PR prevalence and R0 increase monotonically with antibiotic exposure when PR is completely antibiotic-resistant (rR = 1).
source: Like strain competition, microbiome competition underlies a trade-off in antibiotic selection: PR prevalence and R0 increase monotonically with antibiotic exposure when PR is completely antibiotic-resistant (rR = 1) (Appendix 1—figure 1)
evidence: Supported by model results shown in referenced figures.

claim: PR prevalence and R0 can peak at intermediate antibiotic exposure when resistance is partial (0 < rR < 1) because antibiotics simultaneously clear pathogen colonization and induce greater host susceptibility through dysbiosis.
source: but can peak at intermediate antibiotic exposure when resistance is partial (0 < rR < 1) because antibiotics simultaneously clear pathogen colonization and induce greater host susceptibility through dysbiosis (Figure 1I).
evidence: Supported by model results shown in Figure 1I and mechanistic reasoning.

claim: When microbiota simultaneously limit multiple colonization processes (transmission, emergence, persistence), patients with stable microbiota are more protected from PR colonization, but antibiotic use has greater epidemiological costs, selecting more strongly for PR spread.
source: This trade-off is more pronounced when multiple interactions are combined: when microbiota simultaneously limit multiple colonization processes (transmission, emergence, persistence), patients with stable microbiota are more protected from PR colonization, but antibiotic use is predicted to have greater epidemiological costs, selecting more strongly for PR spread (Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: Supported by model results shown in referenced figures.

claim: An increasing rate of within-host HGT (χ) drives increasing PR prevalence (CR), regardless of other microbiome-pathogen interactions.
source: Overall, an increasing rate of within-host HGT (χ) is found to drive increasing PR prevalence (CR), regardless of other microbiome-pathogen interactions (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by model results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Under the modeling assumptions, HGT-driven gains in CR result from symmetric declines in CS, such that HGT's potential impact depends on the presence of both sufficient resistance donors and sufficient recipients.
source: Under our modeling assumptions, HGT-driven gains in CR result from symmetric declines in CS, such that HGT's potential impact depends on the presence of both sufficient resistance donors and sufficient recipients.
evidence: Based on the specific assumptions and structure of the model developed in this study.

claim: Across simulations, C. difficile was the most prevalent pathogen.
source: Across simulations, C. difficile was the most prevalent pathogen (Figure 6A)
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 6A.

claim: MRSA had the highest resistance rate among the simulated pathogens.
source: MRSA had the highest resistance rate (Figure 6B)
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 6B.

claim: ESBL-EC had the highest rate of incidence within the hospital among the simulated pathogens.
source: and ESBL-EC had the highest rate of incidence within the hospital (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 6C.

claim: CP-KP had the lowest prevalence, resistance rate and incidence among the simulated pathogens.
source: CP-KP had the lowest prevalence, resistance rate and incidence
evidence: Based on simulation results.

claim: CP-KP was the pathogen most favoured by the hospital environment, with its prevalence increasing by approximately 5.4-fold (95% uncertainty interval: 2.1–10.9) among hospital patients relative to baseline prevalence in the community.
source: but was the pathogen most favoured by the hospital environment, its prevalence increasing by approximately 5.4-fold (95% uncertainty interval: 2.1–10.9) among hospital patients relative to baseline prevalence in the community (Appendix 1—figure 12A).
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in referenced figures.

claim: For pathogens subject to intraspecific strain competition, resistance rates in the hospital tended to exceed rates in the community.
source: For pathogens subject to intraspecific strain competition, resistance rates in the hospital also tended to exceed rates in the community (Appendix 1—figure 12B).
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in referenced figures.

claim: Patient-to-patient transmission was the primary route of MRSA acquisition.
source: Patient-to-patient transmission was the primary route of MRSA acquisition
evidence: Based on simulation results.

claim: Endogenous acquisition was the primary route for the enteric pathogens C. difficile, ESBL-EC and CP-KP.
source: while endogenous acquisition was the primary route for the enteric pathogens C. difficile, ESBL-EC and CP-KP (Appendix 1—figure 13).
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in referenced figures.

claim: HGT accounted for 8.7% (<0.01–49.7%) of ESBL-EC acquisition events.
source: HGT played a potentially important but highly uncertain role for ESBL-EC and CP-KP, accounting for 8.7% (<0.01–49.7%) and 2.1% (<0.01–22.8%) of acquisition events, respectively.
evidence: Based on simulation results with uncertainty intervals.

claim: HGT accounted for 2.1% (<0.01–22.8%) of CP-KP acquisition events.
source: HGT played a potentially important but highly uncertain role for ESBL-EC and CP-KP, accounting for 8.7% (<0.01–49.7%) and 2.1% (<0.01–22.8%) of acquisition events, respectively.
evidence: Based on simulation results with uncertainty intervals.

claim: In multivariate sensitivity analysis, community prevalence and rates of endogenous acquisition had overall the strongest positive impacts on hospital colonization prevalence across ARB.
source: In multivariate sensitivity analysis, community prevalence (fC for C. difficile, fR for others) and rates of endogenous acquisition (αR) had overall the strongest positive impacts (highest PRCCs) on hospital colonization prevalence across ARB
evidence: Based on multivariate sensitivity analysis results.

claim: Rates of hospital admission/discharge (μ) and microbiome recovery (δ) had the strongest negative impacts on hospital colonization prevalence across ARB.
source: while rates of hospital admission/discharge (μ) and microbiome recovery (δ) had the strongest negative impacts (lowest PRCCs; Appendix 1—figure 14A).
evidence: Based on multivariate sensitivity analysis results shown in referenced figures.

claim: For resistance rates, parameters with the strongest positive impacts were community prevalence (fR), the rate of endogenous acquisition (αR) and the rate of antibiotic-induced pathogen clearance (θC).
source: For resistance rates, parameters with the strongest positive impacts (highest PRCCs) were community prevalence (fR), the rate of endogenous acquisition (αR) and the rate of antibiotic-induced pathogen clearance (θC).
evidence: Based on multivariate sensitivity analysis results.

claim: Parameters with the strongest negative impacts on resistance rates were rates of hospital admission/discharge (μ) and endogenous acquisition of competing drug-sensitive strains (αS).
source: Parameters with the strongest negative impacts (lowest PRCCs) were rates of hospital admission/discharge (μ) and endogenous acquisition of competing drug-sensitive strains (αS) (Appendix 1—figure 14B).
evidence: Based on multivariate sensitivity analysis results shown in referenced figures.

claim: Across ARB, prevalence estimates, but not resistance rates, were generally sensitive to microbiome parameters.
source: Across ARB, prevalence estimates, but not resistance rates, were generally sensitive to microbiome parameters.
evidence: Based on sensitivity analysis results.

claim: Contact precautions were highly effective for reducing MRSA incidence.
source: Contact precautions were highly effective for reducing MRSA incidence
evidence: Based on intervention simulation results.

claim: Contact precautions were of intermediate efficacy for C. difficile.
source: of intermediate efficacy for C. difficile
evidence: Based on intervention simulation results.

claim: Contact precautions were minimally effective for ESBL-EC and CP-KP.
source: and minimally effective for ESBL-EC and CP-KP.
evidence: Based on intervention simulation results.

claim: Contact precautions had comparatively little impact on resistance rates, with a median 2–4% reduction across simulations and compliance levels for MRSA.
source: Contact precautions had comparatively little impact on resistance rates, with a median 2–4% reduction across simulations and compliance levels for MRSA, 0–2% for CP-KP and negligible impact for ESBL-EC (Appendix 1—figure 15).
evidence: Based on intervention simulation results shown in referenced figures.

claim: Contact precautions were overall less effective in microbiome simulations compared to single-species simulations.
source: These interventions were overall less effective in microbiome simulations, which tended to limit the role of between-host transmission (via colonization resistance) and favor the role of endogenous acquisition (via ecological release) in the hospital environment when compared to single-species simulations (Appendix 1—figure 13).
evidence: Based on comparison of simulation results between different model types.

claim: Antibiotic stewardship interventions led to substantial reductions in nosocomial incidence for all pathogens, but only when the microbiome was taken into account.
source: Antibiotic stewardship interventions led to substantial reductions in nosocomial incidence for all pathogens, but only when the microbiome was taken into account (Figure 7).
evidence: Based on intervention simulation results shown in Figure 7.

claim: Stewardship reduced incidence through all acquisition routes, including HGT.
source: Unlike contact precautions, which only reduced incidence via transmission, stewardship reduced incidence through all acquisition routes, including HGT (Appendix 1—figure 16).
evidence: Based on intervention simulation results shown in referenced figures.

claim: Pooling stewardship types together under intermediate compliance, colonization incidence was reduced by a median 20% for CP-KP, 18% for C. difficile, 15% for ESBL-EC, and 10% for MRSA.
source: Pooling these together under intermediate compliance, colonization incidence was reduced by a median 20% for CP-KP, 18% for C. difficile, 15% for ESBL-EC, and 10% for MRSA.
evidence: Based on intervention simulation results.

claim: Single-species simulations excluding microbiome competition predicted negligible efficacy of all stewardship interventions for reducing incidence, and non-efficacy for C. difficile.
source: Single-species simulations excluding microbiome competition predicted negligible efficacy of all stewardship interventions for reducing incidence, and non-efficacy for C. difficile.
evidence: Based on comparison of simulation results between different model types.

claim: Stewardship interventions had a substantial impact on resistance rates, with overall greater reductions for CP-KP than MRSA and ESBL-EC.
source: Stewardship interventions also had a substantial impact on resistance rates, with overall greater reductions for CP-KP than MRSA and ESBL-EC, and similar outcomes across microbiome and single-species simulations (Appendix 1—figure 15).
evidence: Based on intervention simulation results shown in referenced figures.

claim: Microbiome recovery therapy was potentially highly effective for limiting pathogen incidence, but efficacy varied greatly across different levels of intervention compliance.
source: Lastly, microbiome recovery therapy was potentially highly effective for limiting pathogen incidence, but efficacy varied greatly across different levels of intervention compliance (Figure 7).
evidence: Based on intervention simulation results shown in Figure 7.

claim: Microbiome recovery therapy was most effective against C. difficile, of similar efficacy against ESBL-EC and CP-KP, and comparatively least effective against MRSA.
source: This intervention was most effective against C. difficile, of similar efficacy against ESBL-EC and CP-KP, and comparatively least effective against MRSA.
evidence: Based on intervention simulation results.

claim: Microbiome recovery therapy reduced incidence through all acquisition routes but had no clear impact on resistance rates.
source: Across pathogens, microbiome recovery therapy reduced incidence through all acquisition routes,(Appendix 1—figure 16) but had no clear impact on resistance rates (Appendix 1—figure 15).
evidence: Based on intervention simulation results shown in referenced figures.

claim: Simulation results were broadly consistent with previous findings from the literature when microbiome interactions were taken into account.
source: Our simulations predicted colonization dynamics broadly consistent with previous findings from the literature. Input from the community was the main driver of hospital prevalence, and both prevalence and resistance rates tended to increase in the hospital relative to the community, as estimated in previous modeling studies (Knight et al., 2018; MacFadden et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by comparison to published modeling studies.

claim: Findings reflected an important role for between-host nosocomial transmission for MRSA, as observed clinically.
source: Findings reflected an important role for between-host nosocomial transmission for MRSA, as observed clinically (Khader et al., 2019; Nadimpalli et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by comparison to published clinical observations.

claim: Findings reflected a comparatively important role for endogenous acquisition for enteric ARB, as estimated elsewhere.
source: and a comparatively important role for endogenous acquisition for enteric ARB, as estimated elsewhere (Bootsma et al., 2007; Gurieva et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by comparison to published estimates.

claim: Contact precautions were effective for reducing incidence of MRSA and to a lesser extent C. difficile, but had limited impact against Enterobacteriaceae, consistent with clinical trials and modeling estimates.
source: Contact precautions were effective for reducing incidence of MRSA and to a lesser extent C. difficile, but had limited impact against Enterobacteriaceae, consistent with clinical trials and modeling estimates. (Khader et al., 2021; Luangasanatip et al., 2015; Maechler et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by comparison to published clinical trials and modeling studies.

claim: Simulated antibiotic stewardship interventions were broadly effective for reducing incidence across all included ARB, consistent with findings from a meta-analysis of clinical trials.
source: By contrast, simulated antibiotic stewardship interventions were broadly effective for reducing incidence across all included ARB. This is consistent with findings from a meta-analysis of clinical trials evaluating the efficacy of hospital antibiotic stewardship interventions for reducing incidence of ARB colonization and infection (Baur et al., 2017), which we updated to exclude studies co-implementing stewardship with alternative interventions (Appendix 1—figure 18).
evidence: Supported by comparison to published meta-analysis of clinical trials.

claim: Estimates from the meta-analysis predicted the same rank order of efficacy across included ARB as the simulations.
source: In comparison to our findings, estimates from the meta-analysis were associated with greater uncertainty across more heterogeneous interventions, but predicted the same rank order of efficacy across included ARB
evidence: Based on comparison between simulation results and meta-analysis findings.

claim: Meta-analysis estimates showed similar mean efficacy for C. difficile (19% from n=seven studies, vs. 18% under intermediate compliance in simulations), ESBL-EC (18% from n=four studies, vs. 15%) and MRSA (12% from n=10 studies, vs. 10%), but higher efficacy for CP-KP (54% from n=one study, vs. 20%).
source: and similar mean efficacy for C. difficile (19% from n=seven studies, vs. 18% under intermediate compliance in our simulations), ESBL-EC (18% from n=four studies, vs. 15%) and MRSA (12% from n=10 studies, vs. 10%), but higher efficacy for CP-KP (54% from n=one study, vs. 20%).
evidence: Based on comparison between simulation results and meta-analysis findings.

claim: When excluding microbiome interactions, simulations predicted negligible efficacy of antibiotic stewardship interventions for controlling ARB incidence.
source: When excluding microbiome interactions, simulations predicted negligible efficacy of antibiotic stewardship interventions for controlling ARB incidence.
evidence: Based on comparison of simulation results between different model types.

claim: Microbiome competition was found to have a large impact on incidence but comparatively little impact on resistance rates.
source: Here, microbiome competition was found to have a large impact on incidence but comparatively little impact on resistance rates – both for the theoretical pathogen evaluated in Part 1 (Figures 3 and 4) and for the four ARB simulated in Part 2 (Appendix 1—figures 12 and 14)
evidence: Based on simulation results shown in referenced figures.

claim: Stewardship interventions were of similar efficacy for reducing resistance rates across single-species and microbiome simulations.
source: underlying why stewardship interventions were of similar efficacy for reducing resistance rates across single-species and microbiome simulations (Appendix 1—figure 15).
evidence: Based on comparison of simulation results shown in referenced figures.

claim: Strain-based competition explains relative ecological dynamics of co-circulating strains, while microbiome interactions may be better suited to explain how increasing antibiotic use favours ARB incidence.
source: This reflects the importance of different forces of antibiotic selection for different epidemiological outcomes: while strain-based competition explains relative ecological dynamics of co-circulating strains, microbiome interactions may be better suited to explain how increasing antibiotic use favours ARB incidence, and how antibiotic stewardship and microbiome recovery interventions can help prevent colonization acquisition.
evidence: Based on inference from simulation results and mechanistic reasoning.

claim: Microbiome population structure is inherently stable, depending less on the epidemiological transmission of particular taxa, and more on host factors like diet, maternal inheritance, genetics, and antibiotic exposure.
source: By contrast, microbiome population structure is inherently stable, depending less on the epidemiological transmission of particular taxa, and more on host factors like diet, maternal inheritance, genetics, and antibiotic exposure (Brito and Alm, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research on microbiome stability.

claim: Despite great inter-individual diversity in microbiome composition, there is functional redundancy from one host to the next, such that colonization resistance and other forms of microbiome competition are shared across healthy hosts colonized with different taxa.
source: Despite great inter-individual diversity in microbiome composition, there is functional redundancy from one host to the next, such that colonization resistance and other forms of microbiome competition are shared across healthy hosts colonized with different taxa (Bashan et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research on microbiome functional redundancy.

claim: Fecal microbiota transplantation is already used to treat recurrent C. difficile infection.
source: Fecal microbiota transplantation is already used to treat recurrent C. difficile infection, and is under investigation for multidrug-resistant Enterobacteriaceae decolonization (Davido et al., 2019a; Kassam et al., 2013; Saha et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published clinical research.

claim: Fecal microbiota transplantation is under investigation for multidrug-resistant Enterobacteriaceae decolonization.
source: Fecal microbiota transplantation is already used to treat recurrent C. difficile infection, and is under investigation for multidrug-resistant Enterobacteriaceae decolonization (Davido et al., 2019a; Kassam et al., 2013; Saha et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published clinical research.

claim: Cases of donor stool contaminated with toxicogenic and multidrug-resistant bacteria highlight non-negligible risks of fecal microbiota transplantation.
source: Transplantation requires rigorous donor screening and close longitudinal follow-up, and cases of donor stool contaminated with toxicogenic and multidrug-resistant bacteria highlight non-negligible risks (Gupta et al., 2021; Zellmer et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published case reports.

claim: DAV132, when co-administered with antibiotics by the oral route, has been shown to absorb antibiotic residues in the colon and preserve the richness and composition of intestinal microbiota, while maintaining systemic antibiotic exposure.
source: When co-administered with antibiotics by the oral route, DAV132 has been shown to absorb antibiotic residues in the colon and preserve the richness and composition of intestinal microbiota, while maintaining systemic antibiotic exposure (de Gunzburg et al., 2018; de Gunzburg et al., 2015; Pinquier et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published clinical studies on DAV132.

claim: MRSA, C. difficile and ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae are leading causes of antibiotic-resistant and healthcare-associated infection.
source: MRSA, C. difficile and ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae are leading causes of antibiotic-resistant and healthcare-associated infection, while carbapenemase-producing Enterobacteriaceae represent emerging threats of particular concern due to limited therapeutic options for effective treatment of invasive infection (Cassini et al., 2019; Jernigan et al., 2020; Miller et al., 2011; Rodríguez-Baño et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published epidemiological research.

claim: Carbapenemase-producing Enterobacteriaceae represent emerging threats of particular concern due to limited therapeutic options for effective treatment of invasive infection.
source: MRSA, C. difficile and ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae are leading causes of antibiotic-resistant and healthcare-associated infection, while carbapenemase-producing Enterobacteriaceae represent emerging threats of particular concern due to limited therapeutic options for effective treatment of invasive infection (Cassini et al., 2019; Jernigan et al., 2020; Miller et al., 2011; Rodríguez-Baño et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published epidemiological research.

claim: Antibiotic stewardship is a core component of public health efforts to limit the emergence and spread of ARB in clinical settings.
source: Antibiotic stewardship is a core component of public health efforts to limit the emergence and spread of these ARB in clinical settings (Baur et al., 2017), and an important focus of antibiotic resistance modeling (Niewiadomska et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published public health and modeling literature.

claim: Different antibiotics vary in which organisms they intrinsically target, as well as pharmacodynamic factors like route of administration, clearance mechanism and site of absorption.
source: Different antibiotics vary in which organisms they intrinsically target, as well as pharmacodynamic factors like route of administration (e.g. oral vs. systemic), clearance mechanism (e.g. biliary vs. renal excretion) and site of absorption (e.g. small vs. large intestine).
evidence: Based on established pharmacological knowledge.

claim: Differences in antibiotic properties affect the degree to which bacteria in different host niches are exposed to and cleared by different antibiotics, and are increasingly well described.
source: These differences affect the degree to which bacteria in different host niches are exposed to and cleared by different antibiotics, and are increasingly well described (Bhalodi et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research on antibiotic effects.

claim: Asymmetric impacts of different antibiotics on competing commensal and pathogenic bacteria can drive antibiotic-driven selection for high-risk ARB, with important consequences for resistance dynamics and stewardship efficacy.
source: Our findings suggest that asymmetric impacts of different antibiotics on competing commensal and pathogenic bacteria can drive antibiotic-driven selection for these high-risk ARB, with important consequences for resistance dynamics and stewardship efficacy.
evidence: Based on inference from simulation results.

claim: Antibiotics that both disrupt host microbiota and clear drug-sensitive pathogen strains tend to select more strongly for the spread of resistant strains than antibiotics that only target one or the other.
source: Accordingly, antibiotics that both disrupt host microbiota and clear drug-sensitive pathogen strains tend to select more strongly for the spread of resistant strains than antibiotics that only target one or the other (Figure 3).
evidence: Based on model results shown in Figure 3.

claim: Antibiotics with stronger impacts on pathogen clearance (higher θC) lead to increased resistance rates, while consequences for PR colonization prevalence are modest and depend on potential interactions with the microbiome.
source: Overall, antibiotics with stronger impacts on pathogen clearance (higher θC) lead to increased resistance rates, while consequences for PR colonization prevalence are modest and depend on potential interactions with the microbiome.
evidence: Based on model results and analysis.

claim: Antibiotics with stronger impacts on microbiome stability (higher θm) lead to higher prevalence, with only modest effects on resistance rates.
source: Conversely, antibiotics with stronger impacts on microbiome stability (higher θm) lead to higher prevalence, with only modest effects on resistance rates.
evidence: Based on model results and analysis.

claim: Impacts of antibiotic treatment on resistance rates are greater when PR resists a greater share of antibiotics (higher rR).
source: Further, impacts of antibiotic treatment on resistance rates are greater when PR resists a greater share of antibiotics (higher rR), while impacts on prevalence are greater when microbiome-pathogen interactions are stronger (higher ε, η, ϕ) (Appendix 1—figure 4).
evidence: Based on model results shown in referenced figures.

claim: Impacts of antibiotic treatment on prevalence are greater when microbiome-pathogen interactions are stronger (higher ε, η, ϕ).
source: Further, impacts of antibiotic treatment on resistance rates are greater when PR resists a greater share of antibiotics (higher rR), while impacts on prevalence are greater when microbiome-pathogen interactions are stronger (higher ε, η, ϕ) (Appendix 1—figure 4).
evidence: Based on model results shown in referenced figures.
